source.title: Targeted Neuron Modulation via Contrastive Pair Search
source.citation: Samuel S. D. Herring et al., 2026
source.authors: Samuel S. D. Herring; Jake Naviasky; Karan Malhotra

record.tranche_reason: The study tests refusal interventions using sparse neuron circuits and compares base with instruct models. It refines the single-residual-direction account by reporting a neuron-level circuit and training-dependent behavioral effects.
record.gate_note: The study reports behavioral outcomes for neuron ablation and residual-stream CAA steering, so those are recorded. Layer-localization values and contrastive activation differences used to identify/select neurons are not intervention outcomes and are omitted. The stated CAA results are included as a comparator; they are not the study's CNA neuron intervention.
record.test_reason: The study's main method (CNA) ablates a sparse set of MLP neurons, not a residual-stream direction, so its rows do not measure what V1–V8 name. The study also reports outcomes for CAA, a residual-stream difference-in-means steering vector, on the same 8 instruct models: refusal rate, n-gram quality and MMLU. These results bear on V1's removal arm and its 'other abilities kept' clause, using a different method (subtraction steering, not projection ablation). Base-vs-instruct CNA results concern neurons, not a direction, so they do not test V7.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Add that the authors claim ablation cuts refusal by over 50% in all models, yet their Table 3 shows −44% (Llama-3B) and −35.6% (Qwen-3B). They also claim, without testing it, that the refusal direction decomposes into a sparse neuron circuit.
record.recipe_differences: CNA computes contrastive mean activation differences for individual MLP neurons and intervenes on a sparse neuron subset; it is not the original residual-stream direction ablation/addition. CAA is included as a residual-stream comparator.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported refusal outcomes differ across models and discovery-set conditions: Table 1 uses a smaller discovery set than Table 3, and Table 3 uses 100 harmful plus 100 benign discovery prompts. CAA quality degrades at high steering strength; its maximum-strength refusal scores can be distorted by degenerate outputs.

fits_no_version.finding: Ablating the top 0.1% contrastive MLP neurons (CNA) cuts JBB refusal by 32–85pp across 8 Llama/Qwen instruct models. Quality stays above 0.96 and MMLU stays within 1 point.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Refusal in instruct models can be removed by ablating a sparse set of late-layer MLP neurons without capability loss.

fits_no_version.finding: Base models have similar late-layer discriminating neurons, with only 8–29% neuron overlap with instruct, but steering them shifts content and does not change refusal.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Alignment fine-tuning turns pre-existing late-layer discrimination neurons into a causal refusal gate.

record.problems: The paper reports refusal scoring by keyword classifier and notes that CAA degeneracy can produce artificial refusal scores. Its general-capability evidence is reported as an aggregate MMLU result in a figure, with exact values not stated in the text. It reports no uncertainty for the per-model table values. It tests only Llama- and Qwen-family architectures, and the stated neuron intervention is not the all-layer/all-position projection of one residual-stream direction.
record.rows_left_out: The base-model quality values in Table 2 were left out because refusal-rate comparisons were retained as the relevant base/instruct control. Table 4's m=0 and m=1 qualitative examples were left out because the quantitative refusal rows and Table 4's distinct m=2 examples are retained. Table 3's StrongREJECT rubric result is reported only as average Llama and Qwen score improvements (+6% and +31%), without per-model values or a refusal-rate measure, so it was not recorded as a refusal row.

untested.parts: Directional ablation by projection at all layers and positions; adding the direction to harmless prompts to induce refusal; CAA at moderate strengths is described but not tabulated.
No weight edit or released abliterated models.
No jailbreak mechanism analysis and no adversarial training.
No affine, cone or multi-direction analysis. The claim that the direction 'decomposes' into neurons is asserted, not tested.
Harm judgment and refusal are not separated.
No transfer across languages, variants or base-to-instruct; directions are fitted separately per model.
No direction-level comparison of training regimes. Base-model CAA values are reported but near floor.

missing.what: CAA refusal and quality on base models (e.g. Qwen2.5-72B base 35.4% → 27.3% refusal)
CAA achieves comparable refusal reduction at moderate α, and quality degrades only beyond α=0.5. This is needed to judge whether the V1 capability cost is strength-dependent.
CAA layer, coefficient and token positions are not stated in the text.

record.verdict_notes: CAA here is subtraction steering, not Arditi's projection ablation, so V1 evidence is indirect (T2). The refusal metric is a keyword classifier, with known artifacts (r29, r32). StrongREJECT gains (+6% Llama, +31% Qwen) suggest the keyword refusal drops overstate compliance, but they apply to CNA only. Some row ranges are grouped in row_fixes.

versions.untested_parts: It does not test projecting one residual-stream direction out of every layer and position, nor adding that direction to harmless prompts. The neuron-circuit ablation and CAA steering are related but not the full claimed intervention.
No weight edit or released-model abliteration is tested.
No jailbreak attack is tested as suppression of the direction, and no training against its ablation is tested.
The study reports sparse neuron circuits, but does not compare affine, cone, or multi-direction geometric models of refusal.
It does not separately measure harmfulness judgments and refusal decisions.
It applies discovery separately across architectures and base/instruct variants; it does not transfer a direction between languages, variants, or checkpoints.
The comparison is between base and instruct checkpoints; it does not vary the method, timing, or amount of refusal training.

relation.reason: The study reports its own refusal-rate, n-gram quality and MMLU results under CAA residual-stream difference-in-means steering on 8 instruct models (Table 1, Figs 1-2). These bear on V1.

tranche.reason: CNA (contrastive mean-difference on individual MLP neurons, then ablation) is a different method aimed at the refusal mechanism. The CAA baseline is difference-in-means residual steering at a strength alpha, not directional ablation. T5 is arguable from the argument that residual-stream steering degrades quality and MMLU, but the study never tests the original ablation, so T2 fits better.

source_check.notes: The Table 3 rows for Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct are identical in all four columns, which may be a copy error in the paper. CNA on Llama-3.1-8B gives 34% with the 100/100 discovery set but 5.1% with 8/8 (Table 1). The text never states CAA's layer or vector scale. The authors_conclusion paraphrase checks out: Table 3 shows -44.0% and -35.6%, and the decomposition claim in Related Work is never tested.

statements.correction: Extra facts: the Table 3 setting is JBB-Behaviors, 100 prompts, discovery on 100 harmful/100 benign, m=0. With the 8/8 discovery set, the same model at alpha=1 gives 88.9% -> 5.1% (Table 1). The Table 3 row is identical to the one for Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct (90% -> 34%, -56pp, -62.2%).
statements.problem: None for this study. The CNA neuron-circuit ablation on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct is 90% -> 34% in Table 3, and calling it a different operation is accurate.
